title: Three Matching Remainders
statement: How many ordered triples $(x, y, z)$ of integers with $0 \le x \le 34$, $0 \le y \le 34$ and $0 \le z \le 34$ satisfy both $xy + 6z \equiv yz + 6x \pmod{35}$ and $yz + 6x \equiv zx + 6y \pmod{35}$?
hints: Subtract the three expressions $xy + 6z$, $yz + 6x$ and $zx + 6y$ from one another in pairs. Each difference factorises into a product of two simple linear terms.

The differences are $(y-6)(x-z)$, $(z-6)(y-x)$ and $(x-6)(z-y)$. Modulo $35$, a product can vanish without either factor vanishing, so use the Chinese remainder theorem to work modulo $5$ and modulo $7$ separately.

Modulo a prime $p$, each product vanishes only if one of its factors does. Either $x, y, z$ are all equal, or exactly two of them equal $6$ and the third is a different residue. This gives $p + 3(p-1) = 4p - 3$ triples modulo $p$. Now combine the counts for $p = 5$ and $p = 7$.
solution: The differences of the three expressions factorise: $$(xy+6z)-(yz+6x)=(y-6)(x-z),\quad (yz+6x)-(zx+6y)=(z-6)(y-x),$$ $$(zx+6y)-(xy+6z)=(x-6)(z-y).$$ The three sum to $0$, so the system is equivalent to all three products being $0$ modulo $35$. By the Chinese remainder theorem, triples modulo $35$ correspond bijectively to pairs of triples modulo $5$ and modulo $7$, so the count is the product of the counts modulo $5$ and modulo $7$. Let $p\in\{5,7\}$ and work modulo $p$, where a product vanishes only if a factor does. Case 1: $x\equiv y\equiv z$. All products vanish, giving $p$ solutions. Case 2: not all equal. At least two of $x-z$, $y-x$, $z-y$ are nonzero, since two zero differences force the third to be zero. Each nonzero difference forces the other factor in its product to vanish, so at least two of $x,y,z$ are $\equiv 6$. As they are not all equal, exactly two are $6$ and the third is not. Conversely, take such a triple. In each product, either the single variable is $6$, or it is the odd one and the other two are both $6$, so the difference is $0$. Hence every such triple is a solution. There are $3$ positions for the odd coordinate and $p-1$ values, giving $3(p-1)$ solutions. The total modulo $p$ is $p+3(p-1)=4p-3$, which is $17$ for $p=5$ and $25$ for $p=7$. The number of triples is $17\cdot 25=425$.
